claims.title: The coupled spring potential has a local minimum at the origin

passages.quote:
In that file Bjørn Kjos-Hanssen proves in Lean that
$U$ has a local minimum at the origin.

Suppose
that $f$ is analytic at $a$, that the gradient of $f$ at $a$ is zero, and
that the second derivative of $f$ at $a$ is positive definite:

so there is a constant $C>0$ with
$D^2f(a)(y,y)\ge C\lVert y\rVert^2$ for every $y$.

its second-order Taylor polynomial at $a$ approximates it with an
error that is at most $\tfrac12C\lVert x-a\rVert^2$ for every $x$ near
$a$.

So $U$
is analytic at every point.

second_derivative_test_analyticAt.text: Theorem 2.1 and the Lean statement have the same hypotheses and the same conclusion: a finite-dimensional real inner product space, a function analytic at the point, zero gradient there, a positive definite second derivative there, and a local minimum with a weak inequality on a neighbourhood. In the Lean the second derivative enters as the quadratic map sending y to its value at (y, y).

couplingPotential_analyticAt.text: Both say that the potential is analytic at every point of the plane.

couplingPotential_hasFDerivAt.text: Both give the derivative at every point x as the linear map with coefficients 2x₀ + x₁ and x₀ + 2x₁. The Lean writes it as a combination of the two coordinate projections.

couplingPotential_gradient_zero.text: Both say that the gradient of the potential at the origin is zero.

couplingPotential_iteratedFDeriv_two.text: Both give the same formula for the second derivative at every point z and every pair of vectors a and b.

couplingPotential_posDef.text: Both say that the second derivative at the origin is positive definite. The page also notes that the second derivative is the same at every point; the Lean statement is about the origin only.

coupled_spring_potential.text: Theorem 4.1 and the Lean statement both say that the potential has a local minimum at the origin, with a weak inequality on a neighbourhood. Proposition 5.1 on the page says more than this Lean statement: a strict inequality at every other point of the plane. It is not in the author's files, and the two Lean proofs shown here, written for this page, prove it.
